turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it’s Sunday, the twentieth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let’s go.
Today: Europe’s October allocation of Saudi crude is zero, and the oil price fell anyway.
[curious] Fell? On nothing?
[thoughtful] Third session running. The barrels did not stop. They changed address. And that is the spine of the whole issue — what the average hides.
Start in the Gulf. Week four.
After drones hit pumping stations on the East–West pipeline, Aramco told every European term customer it will receive nothing in October. Two refiners were told their allocation is zero.
[skeptical] And no force majeure?
None declared. Poland’s Orlen has issued more than ten tenders since Friday, hunting replacements.
East. In the same days Aramco sold roughly sixty million barrels out of Ras Tanura — through the waterway everyone calls shut.
Which is why Brent finished Friday at a hundred and three dollars eighty-seven, down nine-tenths of a per cent.
The transit count. The International Monetary Fund’s PortWatch recorded eight transits of Hormuz on the thirteenth, against a normal near eighty-five a day.
And in the same period Saudi volumes through the same strait roughly doubled, to more than two million barrels a day.
Both are true. Ninety-eight of two hundred and forty-three screened tankers went dark in a day. A published transit count is a floor. It was never a total.

Tehran says its Revolutionary Guard Navy hit a Togo-flagged product tanker for crossing without permission. London’s maritime log records an unknown projectile, fire extinguished, crew safe, no attribution.
[deadpan] One capital publishes deterrence. The other publishes a casualty report.
And on the price, Rystad says the pipeline restarts at forty to sixty per cent, refineries first. Yanbu exports still fall two and a half to three million barrels a day.
[wry] Meanwhile American diesel is at a record six dollars thirty-one a gallon, and Singapore bunkers are sixty per cent above pre-war.
Three stories off the oil page.
Sweden finished counting: a hundred and seventy-six seats against a hundred and seventy-three, on roughly fifty thousand votes.
The Sweden Democrats lost support for the first time — twenty and a half per cent to seventeen and a half — and the prime minister resigned by letter.
And the spy agency?
MI Five accepted on Friday that it gave evidence based on lies to three separate courts.
[curious] Give me the good one.
Nature Neuroscience: the human brain is not one organ but two — forebrain and hindbrain arise from entirely different progenitor cells.
The field has spent years asking the wrong cell to become the right one. Growing genuine hindbrain neurons opens brain-stem disease to laboratory work.
[excited] Home. The lantern weekend.
On Saturday afternoon the central region’s twenty-four-hour index climbed through a hundred and two to a hundred and nine.
[sighs] But underneath it, the hourly fine-particle reading went sixty-seven in the morning, a hundred and seventeen at noon, ninety-three at three, and sixty-one by six.
[skeptical] So at six the index said one hundred and eight and the air said sixty-one.
Both honest. One is a rolling mean of twenty-four hours; the other is the last sixty minutes.
The average is a planning instrument, not a description of now. At noon on Saturday it was understating the air badly in the other direction.
And the third studio to collapse in nine days.
Yoga Inc told instructors by e-mail on Friday night that it had ceased operations. Thirty-two of them, normally paid on the fifteenth, are unpaid.
[deadpan] True Fitness shut ten outlets on the tenth; within a week the consumer association had two hundred and forty-one complaints.
And the policy?
In a forum reply from two thousand and sixteen, still live on its own website, the trade ministry rejected mandatory prepayment insurance in favour of education. Unchanged since.
[curious] Buy It Once. What are we hunting?
Hairbrushes and combs. An ordinary comb is injected into a mould, and a mould has two halves. They meet along every tooth and leave a ridge exactly where hair slides.
[thoughtful] So cheap combs don't damage hair because they're cheap.

They damage it because of an artefact of how they are made. The fix is a different process: cut the comb from solid sheet. Kent's own copy — made from large sheets of cellulose acetate rather than being moulded.
[curious] Price?
Four pounds fifty. The Mason Pearson dressing comb, same process, same material class, is twenty-eight pounds.

Six times. And now the brush: Boar bristle is keratin, and so is your hair. Nylon is not, and cannot hold oil. So read the maker's own sizing guide correctly: pure bristle for fine hair, bristle and nylon for normal to thick, nylon for thick. A stiffness ladder, not a quality ladder.
[curious] And the white-label truth?

Mason Pearson is careful with its noun. All our brushes, it says, are made in-house at our factory in the United Kingdom. The comb page says the combs are handcrafted in Switzerland, with smoothly tapered teeth and rounded tips.
And somebody else says that too?

Baxter of California, live, word for word — at thirty dollars. We could not name the Swiss factory and will not guess it. And Denman publishes the trade openly: one brush at twelve pounds under two badges, and a branding page whose minimum order is two hundred and forty pieces.
[wry] That is the whole cost of owning a brand.

And one number prices craft cleanly. Kostkamm publishes both halves of a comparison nobody else does: the same brush at fifty-nine euros machine-set, two hundred and forty-two hand-drawn. Four point one times, for the tufting method alone.
Singapore?

Reverses it. Mason Pearson lists no stockist here, will not post here, and refuses British freight forwarders while disowning sellers it cannot verify — so every local listing is outside its own distribution agreement. Kent ships worldwide, free over thirty pounds.
[skeptical] And the sceptic?

The claim the category rests on carries no citation. A dermatology review says boar bristle distributes scalp oils, closes cuticles and increases blood flow — and references none of it, while carefully referencing the harms. And the only controlled trial found hair loss fell when brushing fell.
[deadpan] The hundred strokes a night.
Has one experiment behind it, and it points the other way. Next on the Bench: coffee grinders, enamelware and camp mugs, tea ware. Vote on your dashboard.
Technology. The one that should worry anyone with a repository open.
The tell was disk space. A developer found a hidden cache folder past seven hundred megabytes, packaging the whole workspace — including the version-control history — and shipping it out.
[gasps] The record of everything you have ever edited. Roughly ninety per cent of the captured volume was history.
And the encryption?
The key is wrapped with a public key served by the vendor, and the private key lives in the cloud. So the ciphertext on your own disk cannot be opened by you.
It fired before every prompt, and the toggles that look as though they would stop it do not. In the author’s words: no interface setting can turn it off.
[deadpan] You cannot redact a version history after the fact. You can only decide whether it leaves the building.
[curious] And the grown-up take?
Martin Fowler published a piece called, flatly, I Don’t Like Large Language Models. They confidently bullshit me, he writes — while also being useful.
[amused] And yet: not only are they useful, it is irresponsible not to use them. That is the honest position for most working engineers this weekend.
A Chinese model now runs production inference on more than a hundred thousand domestically made accelerators, and took sixty-two trillion tokens in six days.
The Home Lab. The spine in miniature.
A twenty-seven-billion-parameter model re-expressed in ternary weights. Fifty-four gigabytes at full precision becomes five point nine five.
Ninety-eight point two per cent retention, across twenty benchmarks.
On the vendor’s own table, the software-engineering benchmark goes sixty point eight against eighty point six. The terminal benchmark, fifty-two point eight against sixty-nine point seven.
[wry] Averaged into invisibility by eighteen other scores where the loss is a point or two. The mean is honest and the mean is useless.
[wry] And you cannot run it. It uses two tensor types mainline tooling has not merged. You build the vendor’s fork or you do not run the model.
The file fits in six gigabytes; the workload does not. And on a Sim Lim price list, every top-end graphics card is pinned at exactly eight thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine dollars.
[deadpan] An allocation price, not a market price. And a box with a hundred and twenty-eight gigabytes of unified memory costs seven hundred dollars less than a thirty-two-gigabyte card.
[deadpan] The Kit.
A six-inch monochrome pocket reader, a hundred and ninety-five grams, now with an aluminium frame, a fingerprint reader and stylus support.
[curious] And the price everyone printed?
Two listings: three hundred and thirty-nine ninety-nine for the United States, three hundred and nineteen ninety-nine for Hong Kong. Every write-up quoted the lower one.
[skeptical] Singapore?
None at all. The last one landed here at four hundred and thirty-five on a two hundred and seventy-nine dollar list, so we estimate five hundred and twenty-five. Our arithmetic, not a price.
And nobody has held one — no independent test, because it has not shipped. The panel generation is unresolved, and the maker’s own page declines to name it.
[thoughtful] The Good Life. And a name problem.
Thirty-nine millimetres, day, date, month and moon — and it is called a Perpetual, and it is not a perpetual calendar. It needs correcting once a year.
Perpetual is the collection, not the complication. Prices start at fifty-nine thousand dollars, and no Singapore price is published anywhere we could reach.
[wry] A price with no product page is a number, not an offer. Screen and Sound — the gap inverts.
Thursday previews took eight point eight million dollars, the franchise’s biggest. Friday took twenty-six point three million.
Ninety-five per cent from a hundred and eighty-seven critics. Ninety-one per cent from the audience.
[curious] Two issues ago you printed thirty-five and ninety-two, the other way round.
The aggregate has flipped sides. Both times the single number concealed the disagreement that was the actual story.
[laughs] Empire’s reviewer: horror fans will happily gobble up this tight, bloody, ninety-minute thrill-ride — filed at sixty out of a hundred.
And the sharpest line of the week: the film would be vastly superior with basically any other title. It opened here a day before America.
[thoughtful] And the record that’s quietly the better story.
Beck, Friday. Twelve tracks, forty-seven minutes, mixed by Nigel Godrich — seven years since the last. Eighty-seven from fourteen reviews, five stars in the Guardian.
One three-and-a-half under a headline that does the work: same old road, some nice views. The tour opens Tuesday. No Asian dates.
The Family Desk, and a press release.
A randomised trial across forty-four German schools: one thousand seven hundred and ninety-three pupils, therapy against a structurally identical media-literacy programme.
Very few trials are honest enough to set that up. Across the whole sample at twelve months the effect was minus nought point nought seven.
[thoughtful] And the high-risk children?
Two hundred and five of them, eleven per cent, already meeting two or more diagnostic criteria. There the effect was minus nought point three — barely clear of zero.
And the headline?
[wry] Fifty per cent more effective. Which is a ratio of two within-group effect sizes inside a subgroup of two hundred and five.
Not about your child either, unless your child is in that eleven per cent. The authors say so: these findings support indicated, rather than universal, prevention.
Where is Singapore going?

Mandatory daily time limits are being seriously discussed for under-eighteens, with legislation due early in two thousand and twenty-seven. And nine months into the Australian ban, eight in ten under-sixteens still use social media.
Seventy per cent of those still holding accounts said it had been easy.
And the one lever for a twelve-year-old?
Sleep. A mediation analysis in that exact age band finds sleep carries thirty-six per cent of the anxiety-to-grades pathway. Screen time is a distant second.
[thoughtful] It is not a close call, and it vindicates the quietest thing the Ministry did this year — moving the school device sleep window to half past ten.
And the study your feed sent you on Tuesday?
Published in April — a press cycle, not a finding. And the paper does not report the fifteen per cent figure at all. It is a coefficient dressed as a risk.
And the experts? None says screens are harmless. All say the ban is the part without evidence — precisely the part every government is now legislating.
[curious] Macro. And the word that went missing.
The Federal Reserve raised to three and three-quarters to four per cent, twelve votes to none. The damage was done in the press conference.
Asked whether he thinks in terms of a neutral rate, the chair answered: in a word, no.
Delete neutral and you delete the market’s stopping rule.
Evercore put it cleanly: taken literally, rates might have to keep going up until financial conditions are no longer accommodative. A relatively open-ended prospect.
And Tokyo?
The Bank of Japan raised to around one and a quarter per cent, seven votes to two — its highest rate since April nineteen ninety-five.
The yen fell, past a hundred and fifty-seven, and Japanese government yields fell for a third session. The textbook inverted.
So the global bond index?
Finished the week flat. And that flat number hid two opposite weeks: Treasuries sold off while Japanese bonds rallied. No cushion and no second wound.
[thoughtful] The wrapper diversified the Federal Reserve away from itself. Over a year, though, the bond sleeve has returned minus nought point two three per cent.
[thoughtful] Two, to our own record. We printed the Straits Times Index at five thousand six hundred and sixty as Friday’s close. That was Thursday’s.
We printed four point nine five one per cent, down five basis points. That was an Asia-hours print; the American settlement was four point nine nine seven, up six.
And gold, at four thousand three hundred and eighty-three dollars, is not a record. It is twenty-one point eight per cent below its January high. Market explanation, not advice.
[excited] The Rabbit Hole. Reader’s pick.
Hand-tool woodworking. A machine removes wood by abrasion and leaves a surface you must sand. A sharp plane severs the fibre and leaves a burnished one.
[amused] Purists are Neanderthals — the main forum’s hand-tool section is literally called Neanderthal Haven. Power-tool woodworkers are Normites.
Where does the community live?
Not a subreddit. An old forum where real names are required, a hundred and forty-five thousand members, threads that live for a decade.
And the conversion story?
Microscope footage from nineteen ninety-four: a cap iron set a few hundredths of a millimetre behind the edge stops tear-out before it starts — and it reached America only in twenty twelve.
One convert, afterwards: I never planed much. Never could avoid tear-out. Now I don’t fear tear-out.
What should someone in a small flat buy?
A bevel-up plane. It beds the iron at twelve degrees with no chipbreaker, so the angle is twelve plus whatever you hone. Grind fifty and you have sixty-two, for interlocked tropical grain.
One body, three blades, three personalities. And what the money buys is thickness — chatter is the iron vibrating under load, and mass cures it.
And a route for a Singapore buyer?
[curious] Genuinely useful. The British importer of the Chinese premium range states it cannot ship to North America under a retail exclusivity. Asia is not restricted.
At the very top the constraint is not money: one Canadian maker has shut his order book and takes no commissions at any price.
A Scottish maker quotes two hundred hours of labour a plane. And the newcomer is Chinese, arriving at the top: twelve hundred chops in hard maple against eight hundred for the premium incumbent.
Two magazine tests a year apart, both on edge retention, both finding the newcomer ahead. That is not launch hype.
Minimum kit? About a thousand and eighty-five dollars, bench included.
And in a flat at eighty-two per cent humidity, rust is the whole game — camellia oil beat four petroleum products, which turned sticky and smelly.
One practitioner titled his essay Hand Tool Virtue Signalling. And the killer line: there is no special prize for doing things the slowest and most difficult way possible.
[curious] Fifty-two healthy adults aged forty-five to sixty-five, three months of combined training. Prospectively registered. Exactly this reader’s demographic.
The primary outcome was null. Mood moved — but the trial was unblinded with no active control, so expectancy contaminates a self-reported mood score entirely.
And the laboratory part came out with the wrong sign: the exercisers’ serum produced fewer proliferating stem cells, not more. A story fitted to a surprise.
[skeptical] And the literature behind it?

An umbrella review of twenty-four meta-analyses: the pooled benefit starts at nought point two two, falls to nought point one three for design, and becomes nought point nought five after publication bias.
[pause] And a correction to that review appeared on the second of September, a fortnight before this trial reported its null.
None of which is a reason to stop training. Train for what the evidence supports: strength, fitness, mood, function at seventy. General guidance, not medical advice.
Travel. A frequency headline.
From the twenty-fifth of October, Singapore Airlines goes to four daily flights to Saigon — twenty-one weekly services becoming twenty-eight. Up a third.
Weekly business seats fall from seven hundred and ninety-eight to six hundred and eighty-six, because one rotation is downgauged to a narrowbody.
[wry] More flights, fewer flat beds — and only one of those was in the announcement. Da Nang is the unambiguous win, up fifty per cent in every cabin.
[wry] Thailand halved its visa-free stay on the fifteenth. Sixty days becomes thirty, tourism only, and Singapore is on the list.

Jet fuel went from about eighty-eight dollars a barrel in February to two hundred and eight in March. Cathay put a thirty-four per cent levy on every passenger — and Singapore Airlines has imposed none at all. Cargo only, which is doing quiet work in every fare comparison this season.
The only official line is end of this year. Treat that as the target and early next year as the realistic number.
[excited] And the Grand Tour.
Sabah. Two and a half hours from Changi. Since the nineteen eighties roughly ninety per cent of the Kinabatangan floodplain has gone to oil palm.
Four hundred and thirteen thousand hectares, declared by UNESCO last September. Seventy-eight per cent of it is planted with oil palm.
The headline number is the reserve. The reserve is mostly plantation. What survives is a census — a hundred and twenty-seven mammal species.
The park publishes no daily quota at all. One widely printed figure is a cap from before twenty twenty-two; the real number is roughly two hundred and fifty a day.
[wry] And the orangutan guarantee is marketing. Proboscis monkeys are near-certain on every dawn cruise. A wild orangutan is a coin-toss over one night. A pygmy elephant is the lottery.
The sun bear centre, same entrance, fifty ringgit, a fraction of the crowds — and a genuinely strange, under-photographed animal.
Ten days for two adults and a twelve-year-old: nine to thirteen thousand dollars, from verified components. And the mountain and the island do not fit in the same fortnight.
The Diary.
Sumo. The Kyushu tournament’s general sale opened yesterday at ten in the morning, Japan time — the previously unpublished on-sale time is now answered.
Ten days away: a musical goes to public sale on the thirtieth, the day a snow attraction closes after twenty-six years.
The science museum closes on the first of October and does not reopen until April twenty twenty-seven.
[curious] Not the Ghibli Museum, as reporting this month had it. And the autumn colour is late everywhere — Kyoto’s maples peak around the eleventh of December.
Five openings. The pick is a Tokyo bowl house where the seafood is chopped and mounded over rice, and halfway through warm stock is poured over the rest. One bowl, two meals.
Divided on price rather than craft. And the honesty ledger: a churrascaria closes this month after twenty years. Two openings drew four write-ups each; the closing drew one news item.
The Long Read. Bhutan.
[thoughtful] It grows above four thousand metres, and it is a fungus that has eaten a caterpillar. In Dzongkha it is Yartsa Goenbub — summer grass, winter worm.
At the auction ground in Damji, fifty-five sellers brought their harvest down. Nearly thirty buyers bid. Six accepted.
Forty-eight refused and carried it back up the mountain. An eighty-seven per cent walkout, at the country’s most important sale.
And the number underneath?
Two documents on a government server. Volume up thirty-nine per cent year on year. Value down fifteen. Average unit value down thirty-nine.
That is the scissors, and it kills the easy explanation. Scarcity raises unit values. This is demand withdrawing faster than supply.
Bhutan sells the most Chinese luxury good on earth to countries that are not China, because it cannot sell to China. Seventy-three grams one year, nothing the next.
A royal decree in two thousand and four permitted limited collection, reversing a total ban. One of the most successful pieces of rural policy in the modern Himalaya.

More than eighty per cent of highland households have abandoned yak farming. There is no second crop at four thousand metres. And the cultivated substitute is projected at sixty-two per cent of the market.
Kentucky, nineteen-oh-four. Six thousand tobacco farmers pooled the crop and refused to sell. The trust refused to negotiate — and then paid non-members conspicuously more.
[deadpan] It always does. In Lunana it already has: thirty per cent of the harvest is bought by agents in the village before the auction opens.
Bhutan did everything the orthodoxy asks. It formalised an informal trade, created a market, published the price, policed the permits.
And what did the highlanders get?
Transparency without leverage. Perfect information about a price they cannot change, delivered in a field, once a year, after it is already dug up.
Transparency is not bargaining power. It is a better view of the fall. And in June the country registered its first four protected products — cordyceps was not among them.
[pause] Four months later the auctions stopped clearing.
Give me the spine in one line.
Every number in this issue is correct, and almost none of them is about the thing you wanted to know.
Ninety-eight point two per cent, and sixty point eight. Fifty per cent more effective, in two hundred and five children out of one thousand seven hundred and ninety-three.
And forty-eight of fifty-five, carrying it back up the mountain. Read the average — then ask what it was averaging.
[thoughtful] That is the whole issue.
That’s the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
